Shared Topology vs Contact: Pipe–Flange Static Structural Study
Page 4
Abstract
This project examines how the treatment of the interface between a pipe and two flanges affects the results of a
static structural finite element analysis. A steel pipe (outer diameter 29.80 mm, inner diameter 27.00 mm,
length 225.11 mm) fitted with two eight-hole flanges (outer diameter 60.00 mm, bore 30.00 mm) was modelled
in SOLIDWORKS, prepared in ANSYS Discovery and analysed in ANSYS Mechanical. Two Static Structural
models were built in one Workbench project. Case 1 uses Shared Topology, so the pipe and flanges share
nodes at their interface. Case 2 keeps the pipe and flanges as separate bodies joined by two Bonded contact
regions.
Both cases use Structural Steel, the same body sizing (1.5 mm on the pipe, 3.0 mm on the flanges), a Fixed
Support on the 16 bolt-hole faces and a 500 N Bearing Load in the negative global X direction on one face of
the pipe. The maximum total deformation was 1.212×10−2 mm for Shared Topology and 1.1157×10−2 mm for
Contact (7.95 % difference, Shared Topology as reference). The maximum equivalent (von Mises) stress was
20.357 MPa and 19.548 MPa (3.97 %). The reaction force at the supports was 500.46 N and 500 N. Both peak
stresses are small compared with the 250 MPa tensile yield strength listed in the material data.
The two meshes are generated independently and are not identical, and the contact formulation settings were
not recorded. The observed differences are therefore reported as the combined effect of interface treatment and
mesh, not as proof of one single cause. The report also lists which quantities (for example equivalent elastic
strain and mesh element counts) are not available.
Keywords: Shared Topology, Bonded contact, Static Structural, ANSYS Mechanical, pipe–flange assembly, mesh quality.
1. Introduction
Real structures are assemblies. When an assembly is analysed with the finite element method, the analyst must
decide how neighbouring parts are connected. Two common ways to represent a permanently joined interface in
ANSYS are Shared Topology, where adjacent bodies share faces and therefore share mesh nodes, and
Contact, where the bodies remain separate and a contact definition ties or otherwise governs their interaction.
This project applies both approaches to a simple, well-defined component: a straight pipe with a flange at each
end. The geometry, material, supports, load and mesh sizing are kept the same as far as the software setup
allows, so that the influence of the connection method on deformation, stress and reaction force can be
discussed. The work follows one continuous workflow: CAD geometry → assembly → geometry preparation
→ Workbench setup → Case 1 (Shared Topology) → Case 2 (Contact) → quantitative comparison →
interpretation.
2. Problem Statement

stress and reaction force change when the interface is modelled with Shared Topology instead of Bonded
contact, and what limits the conclusions that can be drawn from such a comparison?

4. Engineering Background
4.1 Finite element method in brief
The finite element method divides a body into elements connected at nodes. Displacement inside each element
is interpolated from nodal values through shape functions, and the element equations are assembled into one
global system. The mesh in this project contains 20-node hexahedral (Hex20) and 15-node wedge (Wed15)
elements, according to the legends of the mesh-quality histograms; both are quadratic elements with mid-side
nodes.
4.2 Static Structural analysis
A static structural analysis assumes that loads are applied slowly enough that inertia and damping can be
neglected. For a linear model the nodal displacements {u} follow from the global stiffness matrix [K] and the
load vector {F}:
[K] {u} = {F}
Strains are obtained from displacement gradients and stresses from Hooke’s law. Results used in this report are
distinguished as follows. Total deformation is the vector magnitude of nodal displacement, directional
deformation is one displacement component (here along global X), equivalent (von Mises) stress is a scalar
measure of the stress state, and reaction force is the force carried by a support. Equivalent stress is defined
from the principal stresses as
σe = [ ½ ( (σ1 − σ2)2 + (σ2 − σ3)2 + (σ3 − σ1)2 ) ]1/2
Equivalent elastic strain is a further standard output, but it does not appear in the solution tree of either model
and is therefore not reported.
4.3 Shared Topology
With Shared Topology, faces that coincide between bodies are shared in the geometry, so the mesher creates a
single set of nodes on the common interface. Displacement continuity across the interface is built into the mesh,
no connection object is required, and the interface can neither separate nor slide. In ANSYS Discovery this is
prepared with the Share Topology tools; the Shared Topology Review shows shared faces in green and
not-shared faces in red.

4.4 Contact-based connection
With contact, each part remains a separate body with its own mesh. A contact region pairs a contact surface
with a target surface, and the solver enforces a relationship between them. Available formulations include Pure
Penalty, Augmented Lagrange, Normal Lagrange and Multipoint Constraint (MPC). A Bonded contact type
allows neither sliding nor separation of the paired surfaces. In this project the contact type (Bonded), scope
mode (Manual), behaviour (Program Controlled) and trim setting (Program Controlled) are documented; the
formulation and the remaining advanced settings are not recorded in this study and are therefore not stated.
Bonded contact and Shared Topology both aim to hold the two surfaces together, but they are not
mathematically identical in general: shared nodes impose continuity by construction, whereas a contact
constraint is imposed between surfaces whose meshes need not match, and its strictness depends on the
formulation and detection settings.

8. Engineering Assumptions
•
The analysis is Static Structural: the load is applied over a single 1 s step and inertia effects are neglected.
•
All three bodies are made of the same isotropic, linear-elastic Structural Steel from the default Engineering
Data.
•
Bolts, nuts, gaskets and any internal fluid pressure are not modelled. The bolt holes are represented by a
Fixed Support on the hole faces, which treats the bolt connection as perfectly rigid.
•
The pipe–flange interface is a permanent, non-separating and non-sliding connection in both cases (Shared
Topology in Case 1, Bonded contact in Case 2).
•
The two cases are intended to differ only in the interface treatment. Mesh sizing, supports and load were set
identically; the meshes themselves are generated independently.
•
Only a Bearing Load and a Fixed Support appear in the Static Structural tree, so no thermal load is applied.

14. Discussion
14.1 Why were Shared Topology and Contact compared?
The interface treatment is a modelling decision made by the analyst, not a property of the structure. For this
pipe–flange assembly both options can represent a permanently joined interface, but they lead to different mesh
topology and different equations at the interface. Keeping geometry, material, supports, load and mesh sizing
the same isolates, as far as the setup allows, the influence of that choice. The comparison is also useful for
workflow: Shared Topology is prepared in the geometry stage, whereas contact is defined in the Connections
folder of Mechanical.
14.2 What changes with Shared Topology?
Adjacent bodies share their interface faces, so the mesh is conforming and the interface nodes belong to both
bodies. Displacement continuity is built into the mesh, no contact definition or contact stiffness exists, and the
model is treated as one continuous solid in terms of connectivity. The trade-off is that the interface can never
separate or slide.
14.3 What changes with Contact?
Each body is meshed on its own, and two Bonded regions (pipe as contact body, flange as target body) impose
the connection between the surfaces. The interface nodes on the two sides need not coincide, so the connection
is an approximate tie between two discretised surfaces, and its strictness depends on the formulation and
detection settings. The 0.10 mm radial clearance between pipe and bore (calculated) is an additional geometric
feature that a contact model has to deal with.
14.4 How does load transfer occur in each model?
In both cases the 500 N load acts on one pipe face, the pipe bends between the two flanges (see the deformed
shapes), and the load reaches the flanges through the pipe–flange interface, then the bolt-hole faces where the
Fixed Support reacts. In Case 1 the load crosses the interface through shared nodes. In Case 2 it crosses through
the bonded contact constraints. The reactions (500.46 N and 500 N) show that the load balance is satisfied in
both models.
14.5 Why might stress and deformation differ?
•
Different mesh. Independent meshing of separate bodies gives a different element set from a conforming
mesh, and the quality histograms differ between the cases.
•
Interface constraint. A surface-based tie across non-matching meshes is not identical to shared nodes.
•
Peak values are local. Maximum stress occurs close to a pipe–flange junction, where stress is sensitive to
element size and shape; small mesh changes can shift a peak by a few percent.
•
Clearance and detection. A 0.10 mm radial clearance may affect which surfaces the contact engages; the
detection settings were not recorded.
Shared Topology vs Contact: Pipe–Flange Static Structural Study
Page 30
14.6 Could mesh differences contribute?
Yes. The two meshes are generated from the same sizing controls but are not identical: Case 2 has a wider
low-quality tail in all three plotted metrics (Table 9). The effect of the mesh cannot be separated from the effect
of the interface without a controlled test, for example a mesh convergence study or a comparison in which both
models use the same mesh.
14.7 Could contact stiffness or formulation affect the results?
In principle yes. Penalty-based formulations use a finite contact stiffness, which allows very small relative
movement between the surfaces, whereas MPC-based bonded contact imposes the connection directly on the
nodes. Because the formulation actually used was not recorded, its influence cannot be quantified in this report.
14.8 What does the comparison say about modelling choices?
For a well-fitting, permanently bonded interface, both approaches give the same global response: the same
deformation pattern, a reaction force that agrees to 0.09 %, and peak values within 8 %. Either would be
acceptable for a first-pass estimate in this case. The peak stress and peak deformation nevertheless move by
several percent, so a peak value should be quoted together with the mesh and connection used. The choice of
connection should be documented, and a peak stress at a junction should not be treated as exact.
14.9 When would contact be required instead of Shared Topology?
•
when parts can separate, slide or rub, for example under frictional or frictionless contact;
•
when the contact status, contact pressure, gap or penetration is itself an output;
•
when bolted joints with pre-tension, gaskets or washers are modelled explicitly;
•
when parts need independent meshes, for example very different element sizes or material regions that are
meshed differently;
•
when the interface geometry does not coincide (clearance or interference) and cannot be made to share
faces;
•
when the model becomes nonlinear because of changing contact conditions.
15. Engineering Interpretation
Both models represent the pipe as a member restrained at the flange bolt holes and bent by a transverse load.
The deformations are very small: the peak total deformation divided by the pipe length is about 5×10−5
(calculated). The peak equivalent stress is about 8 % of the 250 MPa tensile yield strength listed in the material
data (calculated: 8.14 % for Case 1 and 7.82 % for Case 2). A linear-elastic static assumption is therefore
reasonable for this load level, and the material is far from yielding in this simplified model.
The differences between the two interface treatments (3.97 % in peak stress and 7.95 % in peak deformation)
are small compared with the margin to yield in this load case, so the choice of connection would not change a
pass/fail conclusion here. They should not be called significant or insignificant in general, because they depend
on the mesh, on the contact settings that were not recorded and on the purpose of the analysis. The stresses near
the bolt holes and near the pipe–flange junction are idealised by the rigid Fixed Support and by the bonded
interface; they do not represent bolt loads or gasket behaviour.
Both models represent the pipe as a member restrained at the flange bolt holes and loaded along the global X direction.

16. Limitations
•
The comparison is not perfectly controlled. The mesh sizing controls are identical, but the meshes are
generated independently and their quality histograms differ. No mesh convergence study was done.
•
Contact formulation is not documented. The formulation, detection method and interface treatment of the
contacts were not recorded and are not stated.
•
Idealised supports and load. The bolt holes are fully fixed, bolts and gaskets are not modelled, and only
one load case (500 N in −X) is analysed.
•
Thin wall. The calculated wall thickness of 1.40 mm is comparable to the 1.5 mm element size, so the
through-thickness resolution is limited.
•
Single-valued comparison. Maximum values are point values. The reaction force is a global quantity and
the most robust of the compared results.
•
Missing information. The items in Table 10 were not recorded and have therefore not been reported.

17. Conclusion
A steel pipe with two eight-hole flanges was analysed in ANSYS Mechanical under a 500 N transverse Bearing
Load with the flange bolt-hole faces fixed, first with Shared Topology and then with Bonded contact.
•
Both models produced the same qualitative response: a pipe bent between two nearly stationary flanges,

16. Conclusion
A steel pipe with two eight-hole flanges was analysed in ANSYS Mechanical under a 500 N Bearing Load in the
global negative X direction, with the flange bolt-hole faces fixed, first with Shared Topology and then with Bonded
contact.
• Both models produced the same qualitative response: maximum axial displacement occurs near mid-span, while
the flanges remain nearly stationary, and the peak stress in the pipe is located close to a pipe–flange junction.
• The maximum total deformation was 1.212×10−2 mm (Shared Topology) and 1.1157×10−2 mm (Contact), a
difference of 7.95 % relative to Shared Topology.
• The maximum equivalent stress was 20.357 MPa and 19.548 MPa, a difference of 3.97 %; both are about 8 % of
the 250 MPa tensile yield strength (calculated).
• The total reaction force was 500.46 N and 500 N, in agreement with the 500 N applied load to within 0.092 %.
• The two meshes are not identical and the contact formulation was not recorded, so the differences are attributed to
the combined effect of interface treatment and mesh, not to one proven cause.
The study shows that, for a permanently bonded and well-fitting interface, Shared Topology and Bonded contact give
consistent global results. The local peak values should be reported together with the mesh and the connection used.
